Q: Can PolarDB PostgreSQL evaluate a residual predicate on a B-tree index tuple before fetching the heap tuple? A:

This answer is for PostgreSQL. You'll have to verify that PolarDB works the same.

Yes, the filter condition of the index scan can be evaluated before fetching the heap tuple, if all the referenced columns are covered by the index.

Exceptions: columns in the INCLUDE clause cannot be used in that fashion

Q: How should a table reference two columns that have a many-to-many relationship? A:

Presuming your Brands and Suppliers tables are defined as such:

CREATE TABLE Brands (
    ID   INTEGER  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name CHAR(80) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE Suppliers (
    ID   INTEGER  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name CHAR(80) NOT NULL
);

Your bridge table BrandsSuppliers should be constructed this way:

CREATE TABLE BrandsSuppliers (
    BrandID    INTEGER NOT NULL,
    SupplierID INTEGER NOT NULL,

    PRIMARY KEY (BrandID, SupplierID),

    FOREIGN KEY (BrandID)    REFERENCES Brands(ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (SupplierID) REFERENCES Suppliers(ID)
);

We use composite primary key (BrandID, SupplierID) with each component referencing to 2 other table's PKs, that is the simplest way to ensure itself's uniqueness, and it also ensures as long as a row (or pair) in this table exists, the relative brand and supplier must exist. We can of course create its own primary key ID but since this table totally depends on the other two, there's no point to add another new column for such purpose. Also, using a separate stand-alone PK would requires us to add another constraint to ensure the row's uniqueness. (explained below)

And this is how your Products table can directly reference the bridge table (AKA junction table):

CREATE TABLE Products (
    ID         INTEGER  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name       CHAR(80) NOT NULL,
    BrandID    INTEGER  NOT NULL,
    SupplierID INTEGER  NOT NULL,

    CONSTRAINT FK_Product_BrandSupplier
        FOREIGN KEY (BrandID, SupplierID) REFERENCES BrandsSuppliers(BrandID, SupplierID)
);

It's quite straightforward. However, there are times when we need to write queries which need to JOIN between Products and Brands tables, or between Products and Suppliers table. Without direct FK/PK relationship between the two tables, it's still valid to use JOIN clause but it would not leverage the relationship directly. So it would be a better idea to add the FK/PK relationship between Products and Brands, as well as between Products and Suppliers, like so:

CREATE TABLE Products (
    ID         INTEGER  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name       CHAR(80) NOT NULL,
    BrandID    INTEGER  NOT NULL,
    SupplierID INTEGER  NOT NULL,

    FOREIGN KEY (BrandID)    REFERENCES Brands(ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (SupplierID) REFERENCES Suppliers(ID),
    CONSTRAINT FK_Product_BrandSupplier
        FOREIGN KEY (BrandID, SupplierID) REFERENCES BrandsSuppliers(BrandID, SupplierID)
);

Adding the 2 FK references also makes relationship clearer for those who read the schema.

What if BrandsSuppliers has its own PK column

It can have its own primary key, maybe like this way:

CREATE TABLE BrandsSuppliers (
    ID         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    BrandID    INTEGER NOT NULL,
    SupplierID INTEGER NOT NULL,

    FOREIGN KEY (BrandID)    REFERENCES Brands(ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (SupplierID) REFERENCES Suppliers(ID),

    CONSTRAINT UQ_BrandSupplier UNIQUE (BrandID, SupplierID)  -- needed by many-to-many relationship
);

We need to add that UNIQUE constraint to ensure the row (relationship) is unqiue because many-to-many relationship demands that.

And now we might be tempted to change the design of Products table like so:

-- NOTE: this is a bad idea
CREATE TABLE Products (
    ID              INTEGER  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name            CHAR(80) NOT NULL,
    BrandID         INTEGER  NOT NULL,
    SupplierID      INTEGER  NOT NULL,
    BrandSupplierID INTEGER  NOT NULL,

    FOREIGN KEY (BrandID)         REFERENCES Brands(ID), -- Same as before
    FOREIGN KEY (SupplierID)      REFERENCES Suppliers(ID), -- Same as before
    FOREIGN KEY (BrandSupplierID) REFERENCES BrandsSuppliers(ID) -- Changed
);

However, this would bring a new problem. It is highly possible that the certain product could reference to a book not in the brand-supplier relationship, or the supplier is missing in the relationship. This is problematic. We are thus forced to remove those 2 FK/PK relationship and consequently the 2 columns as well, like so:

-- Better, but not good enough.
CREATE TABLE Products (
    ID              INTEGER  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name            CHAR(80) NOT NULL,
    BrandSupplierID INTEGER  NOT NULL,

    FOREIGN KEY (BrandSupplierID) REFERENCES BrandsSuppliers(ID)
);

That means if we need to look up a product's brand info or the supplier info, we must route through the BrandsSuppliers table first. It would be 2 JOIN clauses instead of just 1. So, using composite primary key in BrandsSuppliers table is a better solution.

Q: MSBUILD : error MSB1009: Project file does not exist A:

According to your log and description, seems TFS get command (Get Source Step)erroneously returns “All files are up to date.” and cause the followed MSBuild step failed.

First try following steps to check if it works by set clean during get source:

  1. Modify your definition : In Repository set Clean to True, Clean option to Sources (try to set Source Directory if that not work)
  2. Also enable Clean option for your build solution task

Another possibility is the root sources folder (D:\UAMCAgent\_work\3\s) is not mapped - i.e. workspace does not contain a root mapping.

And suggest you double check the related build account permission, also give it local admin permission on the build agent.

You could disable the default get source steps in the build definition. And use your own script to do the get source/pull files to see if you get the same situation. How to, please follow: Is it able to ignore/disable the first step Get source in vNext Build?

Q: Jenkins and SCP A:

If your goal is just to SCP files generated during the build, and the plugin doesn't seem to be working (I couldn't see anything wrong in your configuration) you can use an "Execute shell" build step and type the scp command something like (try it in a shell first in your job's build directory to get the syntax right):

scp -r build/web-inf/* user@host:/destination-directory

Q: Enabling URL Rewriting with ASP.NET using web.config A:

If you are using a newer version of IIS or using Windows Azure, you don't need the <ConfigSection>. It is built-in in the new IIS. Simply go ahead and use <rewrite> tag directly under <system.webServer> in your web.config.

Q: How is the vector size of std::simd::vec chosen? A:

The standard does not guarantee a specific vector width for std::simd::vec. It only guarantees that the implementation chooses a size that is considered efficient for the target platform.

In practice, implementations typically map the native ABI to the SIMD width they consider optimal for the compilation target. On WASM this is usually straightforward (v128 → 128 bits), while on x86 the selected width may depend on the enabled ISA extensions (SSE, AVX, AVX2, AVX-512) and the library's ABI choices.

So you should not assume that simd::vec<uint64_t> always has 2, 4, or 8 elements. The element count is implementation-defined and may vary across architectures, compiler options, and standard library implementations. Query the type's size or lane count rather than hard-coding expectations.

Q: How can I find a specific consecutive sequence of rows in SQL without MATCH_RECOGNIZE? A:

My other answer shows the straight-forward technical approach. In this answer I will look at the semantics instead.

There is a unix time range in your query: 1755864000 to 1755873000. This is 2025-08-22 12:00:00 to 2025-08-22 14:30:00. One hour and a half. There may be no batteries in this time range, but maybe there are several. You are talking of a large data set, however, so there may be some years of crime events in your table. One hour and a half is a very small range related to that, so we can at least be rather sure that there will be a very small percentage of batteries in that time.

It should hence be the best approach to look for these few batteries first. Then for each of these find the previous two rows and the following one and check their type. I will use a recursive query for this, which is SQL's way to iterate through the rows. As to finding next and previous rows: this should be rather quick, because there must be an index on the timestamp to gurantee uniqueness.

WITH RECURSIVE
  cte (ts_battery, ts, type, id, district) AS
  (
    SELECT ts, ts, type, id, district
    FROM crimes
    WHERE ts BETWEEN 1755864000 AND 1755873000
    AND type = 'BATTERY'
    UNION ALL
    SELECT cte.ts_battery, c.ts, c.type, c.id, c.district
    FROM cte 
    JOIN crimes c 
      ON c.ts =
        CASE cte.type
          WHEN 'BATTERY' THEN (SELECT MAX(c2.ts) FROM crimes c2 WHERE c2.ts < cte.ts)
          WHEN 'ROBBERY' THEN (SELECT MAX(c2.ts) FROM crimes c2 WHERE c2.ts < cte.ts)
          WHEN 'ASSAULT' THEN (SELECT MIN(c2.ts) FROM crimes c2 WHERE c2.ts > cte.ts_battery)
        END
      AND    
        CASE cte.type
          WHEN 'BATTERY' THEN c.type = 'ROBBERY'
          WHEN 'ROBBERY' THEN c.type = 'ASSAULT'
          WHEN 'ASSAULT' THEN c.type = 'MOTOR_VEHICLE_THEFT'
        END
  )
SELECT ts, type, id, district
FROM cte
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT NULL
              FROM cte cte2
              WHERE cte2.ts_battery = cte.ts_battery
              AND cte2.type = 'MOTOR_VEHICLE_THEFT'
             )
ORDER BY ts;

Here is a demo on PostgreSQL https://dbfiddle.uk/Lu6wc-Zh having about 200,000 events from January 2020 to August 2026. The queries in my other answer take about 500 ms, but less than a millisecond when my suggested restriction on the time range gets applied. The query here, too, takes less than 1 ms. It will depend on the actual data which query proves fastest in the end.
